title: The first bat mitzvah (1922)
hookLine: Judith Kaplan becomes a bat mitzvah in New York

lines: A SHABBAT MORNING IN NEW YORK.
A GIRL WALKS TO THE FRONT.
cards: A Shabbat morning in a synagogue in New York, in 1922. The Torah has been read, as it is every week. Then a girl named Judith Kaplan walks up to the front.
Her father is the rabbi, Mordecai Kaplan, and he has decided that what boys do at this age, his daughter will do too. She says the blessings.
She reads a passage of Torah aloud, in Hebrew and then in English, from a printed book. Then she sits down. No party plan, no theme, no DJ.
And with it, the bat mitzvah as many Jews now know it began to take shape.

teach.b: Bar mitzvah, for a boy, and bat mitzvah, for a girl, mean son and daughter of the commandment.

In Jewish law, a child grows into the age of the commandments: from then on, the mitzvot are theirs to keep, not just their parents' to teach. That happens to a girl whether there's a ceremony or not.
Judith Kaplan's Shabbat added a public moment to mark it, in front of the community. And the first one was careful.

teach.h: A PRINTED BOOK, NOT THE SCROLL.
teach.b: She didn't read from the scroll itself, but from a printed book, after the regular reading, standing a little apart. Even so, people noticed.
Her father wanted Judaism to change with the lives Jews actually lived, and a girl standing up in the synagogue was part of that; he later founded the movement called Reconstructionist Judaism.

Then the idea spread, slowly at first, through different movements, each in its own way. Today in Reform, Reconstructionist and Conservative synagogues, a girl may read from the Torah scroll itself, just as a boy does.
In Orthodox communities that mark it, it happens in other ways: a girl gives a talk on a passage she has studied, celebrates with women and family, or takes on a project of learning or kindness.

The Torah itself imagines everyone gathered to hear it: "Assemble the people, the men and the women and the little ones, and thy stranger that is within thy gates, that they may hear, and that they may learn."

teach.h: THAT THEY MAY HEAR, AND LEARN.
teach.b: A girl at a lectern is one way of answering that verse.

how: In Reform, Reconstructionist and Conservative synagogues a bat mitzvah girl may read from the Torah scroll and lead prayers; in Orthodox communities that mark it, the milestone is marked with a talk on a text she has studied, a women's gathering or a family celebration.

games.why: Mordecai Kaplan had Judith say the blessings and read Torah from a printed book, in front of the congregation, on a Shabbat morning.

practice: Remember a girl or young woman who has just done something: started a new school, learned to ride a bike, stood up for a friend, or had her own bat mitzvah.
Hold that moment the way a community holds a girl at the lectern, and notice what she worked for.

wordCard.voice: Bat mitzvah. Hebrew for daughter of the commandment: the day a Jewish girl comes of age to keep the mitzvot, first marked in public by Judith Kaplan in 1922. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: daughter of the commandment, a girl who has come of age to keep the mitzvot.
